issues.description: The problem statement (and UML) consistently refer to a Meal class (with name and ingredients), but the template repository does not provide a Meal implementation. Instead the template contains an Order class with the same shape. This type/name mismatch between the expected type (Meal) and the provided type (Order) will confuse students: they will look for and be instructed to use Meal but only find Order (and an empty Meal.java). The solution repository uses Meal, matching the problem statement, which shows the template is structurally inconsistent with both the problem and the solution.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the template consistent with the problem statement by providing a proper Meal class implementation in the template (matching the solution's Meal: name, ingredients, constructor, getters). Remove or rename the redundant Order class or adapt references in the template to use Meal. Ensure Main and any example code reference Meal rather than Order so students find the expected class and API.

issues.description: The problem statement and the solution refer to the core entity as Meal (a class representing a meal with ingredients), but the template repository provides an Order class with the same structure and role. This mismatch (Meal vs Order) creates a mapping barrier: students reading the problem will look for a Meal class and related usages, but the starter code exposes Order, which may cause confusion about which class to implement, rename, or use.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the identifier consistent across artifacts. Update the template to provide a Meal class (rename Order.java to Meal.java and the class to Meal, or add a Meal wrapper delegating to Order) and adjust all references in the template (e.g., Main) to use Meal. Alternatively, change the problem statement to refer to Order everywhere, but aligning the template to the problem (providing Meal) is recommended.
